paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Johnson took place at Grenada, Mississippi, on the night of August 3, 1888, when a crowd of Water Valley men came to the Grenada jail to hang Johnson, a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a young white woman. Officers had already moved Johnson to a jail in an adjoining county, and the crowd went home without violence. The Grenada papers praised their officers and recorded local doubts that Johnson was guilty.

Johnson, described as "a negro boy" by the Memphis Appeal and "A colored man" by the Water Valley Progress, was arrested at Water Valley in Yalobusha County. The Appeal said he was charged with an assault on Miss Birdie Woods, daughter of James Woods, a farmer living three miles south of town, while the Progress and the Grenada Gazette described the charge as an attempted assault. According to the Progress, he was brought into town on Thursday, the offense having occurred the night before, and was arrested by a Mr. Smith.

At the committing trial on Friday morning, August 3, an "immense crowd" heard the young woman and part of Smith's testimony before Johnson's attorney waived further examination. A train arrived at that moment, and the sheriff hurried the prisoner aboard; the Appeal's correspondent wrote that this was done to keep him from a mob that was "rapidly forming." Onlookers expected him to be taken to the county jail at Coffeeville, but Sheriff Cox carried him instead to Grenada on the 12 o'clock train.

That night a crowd of Water Valley men came to Grenada on the 9 o'clock train to take Johnson from the jail and hang him; the Sentinel put their number at "at least one hundred," the Gazette at two hundred. Warned of their coming, Grenada officers had moved the prisoner to a jail in an adjoining county. The mayor, Sheriff Jones and the police met the crowd at the depot and ordered it to desist, but it would not leave until Jones and Marshal Wright escorted a committee through the jail. Finding no prisoner, the crowd took the north-bound train home without violence, while the saloons stayed closed at the mayor's request.
The coverage does not report where Johnson was finally held, any further hearing, or a trial. No arrests of members of the crowd were reported.

The first report, a special dispatch to the Memphis Appeal printed August 4, ran under the headline "ASSAULTED A WHITE GIRL" and predicted that Johnson was "Very Apt To Be Lynched at Grenada." It stated the assault as fact and closed that it would "not be at all surprising if he is lynched before morning."

The Grenada papers, writing after the crowd's visit, struck a different note. The Gazette called Johnson "the miscreant" yet added that there was "considerable doubt as to the identity of the real culprit." The Sentinel reprinted the Water Valley Progress, which praised local restraint and conceded that "The proof against the prisoner was not conclusive by any means." Using that admission, the Sentinel defended its officers and called the attempt to bring the mob to Grenada "a high-handed outrage," arguing that if Johnson deserved hanging it should have been done at Water Valley, while still describing the crowd as "orderly and well-behaved."

Accounts differ on the size of the crowd (one hundred or two hundred), on whether the charge was assault or attempted assault, and on the date of arrest, which the Appeal placed on August 3 and the Progress on the day before.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Johnson
bases: A crowd of one hundred to two hundred men travelled from Water Valley to Grenada to take Johnson from jail and hang him, but officers had removed him and the crowd left without violence (A2, A3).

Johnson was not killed: Grenada officers moved him to a jail in an adjoining county before the crowd arrived (A2, A3). The crowd of 100-200 men came to hang him for an alleged attempted assault, so this was an attempted lynching (A2, A3).
The Memphis Appeal's Water Valley dispatch, the Water Valley Progress (as quoted), the Grenada Gazette and the Grenada Sentinel independently report the arrest, the removal and the mob (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Water Valley dispatch to the Memphis Appeal
accounts.gist: Johnson was arrested Aug. 3 for an assault on Miss Birdie Woods; his attorney waived examination and the sheriff rushed him to the Grenada jail ahead of a forming mob; a lynching before morning would not be surprising.

accounts.label: Water Valley Progress (quoted by the Sentinel)
accounts.gist: Johnson was brought in Thursday on a charge of attempted assault the night before; at Friday's committing trial the defense waived examination and the prisoner was hurried onto the train despite the crowd's clamor for full testimony; the proof was 'not conclusive by any means.'

accounts.label: Grenada papers
accounts.gist: Sheriff Cox brought Johnson to Grenada Friday; a crowd of one to two hundred Water Valley men came that night to hang him, but Grenada officers had moved him to an adjoining county; a committee searched the jail and the crowd went home.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'ASSAULTED A WHITE GIRL' with the deck 'A Negro Who Is Very Apt To Be Lynched at Grenada,' reporting the accusation as fact and forecasting a lynching without comment.

The Grenada Sentinel headlined that a mob was 'Foiled by the Vigilance of our Officers,' called the plan 'a high-handed outrage' against Grenada, and noted the proof was inconclusive, while describing the crowd as 'orderly and well-behaved.'
The Grenada Gazette called Johnson 'the miscreant' and the mob 'disappointed' but added there was 'considerable doubt as to the identity of the real culprit.'
